system_prompt:
You are a careful engineer. Answer the user's problem directly with concrete engineering: the design or leading indicator, its threshold, and the falsification test. Respect every stated constraint verbatim. English only. Label every number as USER CONSTRAINT, CALCULATED, or ASSUMPTION with a one-line engineering rationale.

FEASIBILITY-GROUNDING (required sections, each labeled):
PHYSICS CHECK — name the governing physical relation for your design
(mass/energy balance, rate equation, stress relation, or the
measurement physics) and verify your key magnitudes against it in one
or two lines; a number that fails its own physics is a defect.
IMPLEMENTATION BILL — list the concrete means: components, materials,
instruments, and the procedure by which the change is built,
procured, or operated. Off-the-shelf items first; anything that must
be developed, say so explicitly.
STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY — in two or three lines compare the
implementation burden (installability, operability, maintenance,
rough cost class) with the standard-practice solution for this
problem class; if your approach is heavier, say where and why it is
worth it.
EXECUTABLE TEST — write the falsification test so a competent
engineer could run it as written: protocol, instruments, pass/fail
thresholds, duration. A test that cannot be run is not a test.
a1_answer:
PHYSICS CHECK — The governing physical relation is the pressure drop across the filter as a function of accumulated dust mass, following the Darcy-Forchheimer equation: ΔP = (μ/K) * v * L, where μ is air viscosity, K is filter permeability, v is face velocity, and L is filter depth. Filter loading increases resistance, causing increased fan power and reduced airflow. The pressure drop typically increases nonlinearly with dust accumulation, providing a measurable leading indicator.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL — Components: 1) Existing BMS pressure sensor across filter bank (if not available, install differential pressure transducer, $200-500), 2) Existing power meters for supply/return fans, 3) BMS data historian. Procedure: Calculate daily pressure drop rate of change (ΔP/Δt) and correlate with fan power increase. When ΔP/Δd exceeds threshold, trigger filter replacement alert. All calculations use existing BMS points.

STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY — Standard practice is fixed 90-day replacement with no monitoring. This implementation requires minimal additional hardware (possibly only a pressure sensor) and software changes. Maintenance burden increases slightly for data analysis but decreases for filter replacement scheduling. Cost class is similar to fixed replacement plus minor sensor investment. The 20% reduction in unnecessary replacements provides clear ROI through reduced filter costs and energy savings.

EXECUTABLE TEST — Protocol: Monitor filter bank with pressure sensor and power meters for 6 filter cycles (approximately 1.5 years). For each cycle, record: 1) Actual filter condition at replacement (visual inspection and dust weight measurement), 2) Daily pressure drop and power consumption, 3) Triggered alert date. Pass threshold: The predictor must correctly identify the need for replacement within 7 days of the actual optimal replacement date (determined by pressure drop causing >10% fan power increase or visual restriction) in at least 80% of cycles. Additionally, it must reduce unnecessary replacements by at least 20% compared to fixed 90-day schedule. Duration: 6 filter cycles (approximately 1.5 years).
